RECOMMENDED PROGRAM OF INSTRUCTION

     3-203. The program starts with training done routinely while at home station as part of the normal training
     cycle. This training includes academic and flight training and defines the train-up of personnel upon
     notification of deployment. Outside experts may conduct training for the unit.

Academics

     3-204. Suggested topics include—
          • Human factors associated with overwater flying.
          • Environmental factors that affect overwater operations.
          • Principle difficulties during overwater operations.
          • Overwater aviation life support equipment requirements.
          • Water survival.

Flight

     3-205. Flight training may be limited by conditions at the unit's home station. Some areas may not be able to
     replicate conditions adequately for training. Instructors can demonstrate techniques and procedures to some
     extent. Crews are evaluated on these procedures during their APART or no-notice evaluations. Flight
     simulators are also a great device in training for this environment.

SECTION VI – DEGRADED VISUAL ENVIRONMENT

     3-206. Degraded visual environments (DVEs) can be caused by numerous environmental factors. They are
     not unique to any geographic location and the challenges are factored into every flight as it can lead to spatial
     disorientation and loss of control inflight.

ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS

     3-207. Everywhere we fly poses the potential for a DVE that we must be prepared to operate in. The
     preconditions that can cause a DVE and lead to spatial disorientation are broad and encountered often.

ADVERSE WEATHER

     3-208. Weather conditions that lead to DVE can be experienced in any climate. These factors should be
     considered during the planning process to combat their effects and ensure mission execution. Factors included
     are:

          • Low visibility.
          • Fog.
          • Rain.
          • Mist.
          • Haze.
          • Dust.
          • Snow.
          • Smoke.

LOW CONTRAST CONDITIONS

     3-209. Low contrast conditions are predominantly encountered at night. These factors, combined with low
     illumination, can pose a deadly risk:

          • Sunrise/sunset.
          • Moonrise/moonset.
          • Smooth, glassy water.
          • Low illumination.
          • Lack of cultural lighting.
          • Ground lights.

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  141


---

Chapter 3

          • Night unaided flight.

LOCAL WEATHER PHENOMENON

     3-210. On a micro-level environment, local weather phenomenon can be encountered that are DVE events
     or can lead to them. These can cover a large geographic region or a smaller section based on terrain or other
     features.

          • Marine layer fog.
          • Valley fog.
          • Mountain wave turbulence.
          • Santa Anna winds.

SPATIAL DISORIENTATION PREVENTION

     3-211. When operating in a degraded visual environment, the aircrew is susceptible to spatial disorientation
     and subsequently loss of control inflight. The best tactic to avoid/mitigate the effects of DVE is through
     anticipation and avoidance. Communication provides the ability to apply crew coordination to the potential
     spatial disorientation situation. In the event the crew succumbs to spatial disorientation, counteract is a
     proactive process to save the aircraft and regain orientation.

     3-212. Anticipate-this phase occurs before takeoff during planning and preparation as well as reassessed
     throughout the flight to ensure conditions are as planned.

          • Assess the conditions.
          • Develop en route decision triggers (EDTs).
          • Discuss the use of aircraft systems and automation to avoid spatial disorientation.

     3-213. Avoid-As conditions change, continuously revise the plan. Proactively avoid spatial disorientation
     with increased vigilance, amplified crew coordination, and sound aeronautical decision making.

          • Evaluate the plan.
          • Execute EDTs.
          • Trust your instruments/delay intuitive action.
          • Maintain stable flight.

     3-214. Communicate-Army pilots are hesitant to communicate when they are having difficulty controlling
     the aircraft or experiencing possible spatial disorientation. Extraneous conversation can be as dangerous as
     under communicating. Implement a sterile cockpit during conditions that demand high attention. The pilot
     on the flight controls will announce "UNCAGED" in the event they experience spatial disorientation.

          • Announce.
          • Early communication.
          • Cross monitor.

     3-215. Counteract is a proactive reaction to spatial disorientation preventing an unusual attitude.
          • In the critical moment, a practiced instinctive response to counteract an unusual attitude before a
                loss of control
          • Practice unusual attitude recovery until it is a trained instinctive response. This is accomplished
                through crew awareness and maneuver training.
          • This takes practice both in the aircraft and the simulator. Do a good job. This maneuver is not an
                afterthought in the downwind.

FLYING TECHNIQUES

     3-216. Flight operations in a degraded visual environment can prove challenging for any aviator, regardless
     of experience. Aviators should be prepared when encountering conditions conducive to spatial disorientation.

SPATIAL STRATEGIES

     3-217. Transitioning from an environment that requires reliance on outside visual cues to an environment
     that requires sole reliance on instruments can easily lead to spatial disorientation if one is not prepared for it.

142  TC 3-04.1-4  18 March 2026


---

                                                                                                      Rotary-Wing Environmental Flight

     Understanding spatial strategies can prepare the aviator for these transitions as well as preventing a startle
     response.

     3-218. To develop spatial strategies that help prevent disorientation, crewmembers must fully understand
     how the thought process changes when switching between spatial strategies. The two most important factors
     to resolve when analyzing any spatial perspective are identification of primary spatial cues and determination
     of their relative motion.

OUTSIDE SPATIAL STRATEGY

     3-219. When a view of the horizon is available, aviators will rely upon the outside spatial strategy to maintain
     orientation. The horizon or terrain provide the primary spatial cue, and the aircraft instruments are the
     secondary spatial cue. As conditions deteriorate and maintaining orientation with outside spatial cues
     becomes more challenging, the aviator may become so focused that they exclude a crosscheck inside. This
     can cause the aviator to delay the transition to instruments and it becomes a sudden reaction, eliciting a startle
     response and leading to the potential spatial disorientation or worse, loss of control inflight (LOC-I).

INSIDE SPATIAL STRATEGY

     3-220. When adequate outside references unavailable, the primary spatial cue becomes the attitude indicator
     and other instrumentation. As conditions deteriorate and the focus becomes the instruments, the pilot is no
     longer utilizing the outside spatial strategy and must transition to an inside spatial strategy. This means that
     the pilot is aware that adequate outside references are unavailable and must rely on flight instruments to
     maintain control of the aircraft. If it is necessary to attempt outside reference (instrument approach), this
     should be done by the pilot not on the flight controls. Non-rated crewmembers should maintain situational
     awareness and provide airspace surveillance when required.

FORMATION SPATIAL STRATEGY

     3-221. Formation strategy is utilized by the trailing aircraft in multi aircraft operations. The preceding aircraft
     becomes the primary spatial cue, and the horizon and/or terrain becomes the secondary spatial cue. In a
     degraded visual environment, the instrumentation may be

EN ROUTE DECISION TRIGGERS

     3-222. During the planning process, aviators can anticipate the conditions that will lead to a degraded visual
     environment. En route decision triggers (EDTs) are a predetermined set of conditions that trigger an action
     that was planned briefed and reviewed by the briefer. Crews should be able to discuss how weather,
     environment, and modes of flight may affect their visual perception of the surrounding terrain. During the
     planning process, crews should be able to discuss where disorientation is likely, why they expect that area to
     be hazardous, and how to properly react to spatial disorientation once encountered. The mission briefing
     officer and final mission approval authority are included in this during the mission approval process. EDTs
     are an environmental CAUTION or WARNING light that demand a preplanned response.

     3-223. The three most common triggers are location, airspeed and altitude. Additional considerations should
     be whether the operation is in a permissive or non-permissive environment. Reactions to the trigger may
     require the flight to turn around, land or commit to instrument meteorological conditions (IMCs). The
     reaction is part of the EDT and are discussed and decided upon during the mission approval process and
     included in the crew brief. Timely, controlled reactions to triggers will save lives.

TRIGGERS

     3-224. During the planning process, identify a location or locations to use as decision triggers. This creates
     a point that the flight does not proceed further based on the weather conditions encountered. The decision
     could be based on fuel and the required fuel to return to a forward arming and refueling point or other refuel
     location, ability to divert to a suitable facility, or limiting terrain such as mountains or overwater.

     3-225. Airspeed is an indicator and a trigger for when the environment is no longer sustainable for flight
     operations. When the environment begins to degrade, airspeed should be reduced as needed for the
     conditions. At a certain speed reduction, this should become the enroute decision trigger. Such as, if the

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  143


---

Chapter 3

     environment requires the flight to slow to 80 KIAS in cruise, at that point, the flight executes a preplanned
     reaction.

     3-226. Altitude based on the forecast and approved ceiling minimums with knowledge of the terrain is an
     enroute decision trigger. The aviator will base this off what was the planned altitude for the flight as well as
     what was approved on the risk assessment.

REACTIONS

     3-227. The most obvious reaction will be to turn around. This depends on multiple factors; the aviator must
     determine if the weather that was passed through still sufficient. Additional considerations will be if weather
     is expected to improve and in what proximity and how enveloped is the flight. A turn requires additional time
     and space that may make it no longer an option. Delaying a reaction can cause the flight to get boxed into a
     situation that makes other reactions no longer feasible.

     3-228. If METT-TC allows for a permissive environment, LAND THE HELICOPTER. Often flights that
     occur in degraded visual environments and result in spatial disorientation give up suitable LZs in favor of
     trying to continue the flight. Aviators often choose not to land because they are worried about the scrutiny
     they would incur for making a precautionary landing or they are fixated on completing the mission, making
     it to the destination, or back to base.

     3-229. Delaying the decision to execute a reaction can elicit a startle response, making IIMCs an even more
     dangerous situation. Committing to IMCs in response to a trigger allows the pilot to remain in control of the
     decision and reduces the pressure in the cockpit. The aviators must consider IFR planning factors when
     determining to use "commit to IMCs" as the primary reaction.

OPERATIONAL CONSIDERATIONS

     3-230. The degraded visual environment requires additional awareness as well as more involved planning
     and incorporating flying techniques used in other environments to prepare for the effects and the aviator must
     train to operate in degraded visual environments.

TAXIING AND TAKEOFF

     3-231. Degraded visual environments may be increased during the takeoff portion of flight, due to high power
     settings that generate blowing debris, sand, snow, or other items. If visibility is available to view obstacles,
     the aviator can accomplish takeoff as a day VMC takeoff and apply spatial strategies as necessary, prepared
     to transition when appropriate. If the visibility in insufficient, the takeoff should be performed as an ITO.
     Depending on how degraded the visual environment is, the pilot not flying may either focus on the
     instruments and crosscheck the spatial orientation of the pilot flying or maintain an airspace surveillance to
     ensure obstacle clearance.

EN ROUTE

     3-232. Crews should understand employment of the different spatial strategies as required to maintain
     orientation while flying in a degraded visual environment. Once enroute, crews need to ensure they do not
     exceed pre-determined enroute triggers and must continuously discuss current conditions and be prepared to
     deviate if conditions deteriorate earlier than anticipated. To maintain clear situational awareness for the entire
     crew and ensure the flight proceeds as planned, continuous communication is essential. This constant
     dialogue allows for early detection and mitigation of spatial disorientation in any crew member.

LANDING

     3-233. Landing in degraded visual environments presents a significant challenge due to unfamiliarity with
     landing zones and the combined effects of high-power settings, formation flight, and airborne debris like
     sand or snow. These factors increase the risk of spatial disorientation. To mitigate this, pilots should employ
     scanning techniques such as inside-out scanning, maintain strong crew coordination, and diligently monitor
     flight instruments. Furthermore, crews must possess a thorough understanding of wind effects on landing,
     particularly in formation, to ensure a safe and successful touchdown.

144  TC 3-04.1-4  18 March 2026


---

                                                                                                      Rotary-Wing Environmental Flight

MAINTENANCE

     3-234. Optimal aircraft preparation is crucial for mitigating the hazards of DVE, to include the following:
          • Windscreen Condition: Ensure windscreens are spotless, as dirt or streaks can exacerbate the
                visual distortions inherent to DVE.
          • Instrument Integrity: Any malfunctioning aircraft instrumentation poses a heightened risk during
                DVE operations. Conduct a thorough assessment to determine if the malfunction presents an
                unacceptable hazard for flight in such conditions.
          • Operational Lighting: Verify that all aircraft lighting systems, both internal and external, are fully
                functional. Proper lighting is essential for maintaining spatial orientation and visibility during DVE
                conditions.
          • Terrain Awareness Systems: Confirm the full functionality of all terrain awareness and warning
                systems, including enhanced ground proximity warning system and terrain banding, to provide an
                extra layer of safety and situational awareness in DVE.

TRAINING

     3-235. Training for DVEs will be conducted at the unit with annual spatial disorientation training as specified
     in the applicable publication. Additional training should be conducted and included in every training event
     to the maximum extent possible.

ACADEMICS

     3-236. Recommended topics include—
          • Human factors with degraded visual environments.
          • Spatial disorientation.
          • Environmental factors.
          • EDTs.
          • Spatial strategies.

SCENARIO-BASED TRAINING

     3-237. Training may be conducted in the simulator utilizing scenarios to incorporate aeronautical decision
     making, the development and execution of EDTs, hands-on recovery, recovery using automation and IIMC
     training. Mission planning should incorporate the mission planning process to help develop junior aviators
     understand the decision-making process necessary for EDT development.

     3-238. Commercial-off-the-shelf vision restriction devices can be used in the aircraft to execute scenario-
     based training. Units should develop a SOP incorporating these devices prior to using them in the aircraft.

MANEUVER-BASED TRAINING

     3-239. Maneuver-based training is based on the aviator's experience and ability to manipulate the aircraft
     with the goal being response to spatial disorientation and unusual attitude. The aviator should be trained to
     be comfortable under controlling the aircraft under VMCs and simulated IMCs. As the aviator demonstrates
     mastery in control of the aircraft, training will be conducted to simulate unusual attitude recovery. The initial
     iterations will be low magnitude moving to more complex, greater magnitude, and multi-axis recoveries.
     Evaluations will be conducted according to the applicable aircrew training manual.

                                                 Chapter 4

                        Rotary-Wing Night Flight

    Day or night, vision is the primary sense providing crewmembers with awareness of aircraft
    position or SA. Eyes can rapidly identify and interpret cues in daylight. During darkness, visual
    acuity decreases proportionally as the level of illumination decreases. NVDs improve the
    capability of the human eye to see at night but still suffer from limitations as conditions
    deteriorate. This chapter covers NVDs and provides a general discussion of night vision and
    techniques for completing missions safely.

SECTION I – UNAIDED NIGHT FLIGHT

     4-1. In today's aviation environment, night missions are seldom conducted completely unaided. There are
     times, however, that aviators may determine that unaided flight is preferable to aided flight. There are definite
     reasons for doing so, as well as some potential problems that need to be avoided. The basic principle is to
     choose the sensor that is most appropriate for the mission and flight environment.

     4-2. Generally, aircrews should only go unaided when the light level is very high (usually 75 percent or
     above), when the advantages of a full field of view and color perception outweigh the limitations of reduced
     or uneven light levels. This occurs most often when there is a significant amount of cultural lighting, such as
     in a city or at an airfield. This is a decision the PC of the aircraft must make in accordance with the unit SOP.

PROBLEMS

     4-3. One of the biggest problems with unaided flight is that dark areas can be difficult or impossible to see
     into. The level of available detail is inconsistent due to the highly variable light level. Obstacles can be very
     difficult to see. Additionally, the flight environment (visibility or weather) may change while the aircrew is
     effectively "heads down" in the lighted area.

CONSIDERATIONS

     4-4. The following are considerations of unaided night flight: cockpit lighting, altitude/airspeed changes,
     glasses, and dark adaptation.

COCKPIT LIGHTING

     4-5. Cockpit illumination should be kept at the lowest level consistent with safe operation of the aircraft
     (figure 4-1, page 148). This does not mean 'as dim as possible.' As ambient level decreases from twilight to
     darkness, intensity of the cockpit lights should be continually reduced to a low, usable level, reducing any
     glare or reflection off the windscreen. Cockpit instruments should be instantly and easily readable. The delay
     required for aviators to adapt their vision to cockpit illumination levels that are too low can result in
     unacceptable loss of situational awareness, particularly at NOE altitudes. Crewmembers should be discreet
     in the use of supplemental lights to avoid detection by enemy forces.

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  147


---

Chapter 4

                                                   Figure 4–1. Cockpit lighting

ALTITUDE/AIRSPEED CHANGES

     4-6. During unaided flight operations, allow time to adjust to flight conditions. This includes readjustment of
     instrument lights and orientation to outside references. During the adjustment period, the aircrew's night
     vision continues to improve until optimum night adaptation is achieved. Remember to allow additional time
     and distance to allow for reduced ability to identify landmarks and obstacles. It is important to recognize the
     level of one's ability to accurately interpret the terrain. It may become necessary to slow down or increase
     altitude to allow the reaction time necessary to react to changes. It is much easier to out-fly one's ability to
     see unaided than when using an NVD.

GLASSES

     4-7. Many people suffer from slight visual defects. The importance of correcting for these becomes greatly
     magnified when operating in marginal conditions, such as limited visibility or unaided flight. Remember to
     keep them clean.

DARK ADAPTATION

     4-8. Vision is possible due to chemical reactions within the eye. Night vision requires a buildup of one of
     these chemicals (Rhodopsin) in the rod cells in the retina. The average time required to attain peak sensitivity
     or adaptation to a dark environment is 30 to 45 minutes. Depending upon the individual's starting level, dark
     adaptation is about 80 percent complete within 30 minutes, but it may take hours or even days to reach
     individual maximum dark adaptation. Full dark adaptation never really occurs in the cockpit because of the
     light intensity provided by instrument lights. The physiological processes involved are fully explained in TC
     3-04.93.

Sunglasses

             Note. Colored sunglasses DO NOT protect dark adaptation.

     4-9. For sunglasses to be effective, all visible light has to be attenuated, not just portions of the visible
     spectrum. Colored or yellow visors and spectacles do not protect dark adaptation. To protect unaided night
     vision, allow for scanning close to the sun, and provide normal color vision, use dark sunglasses with a neutral
     gray tint. Tinted sunglasses that are too dark may reduce visual acuity unless the ambient brightness remains
     excessively high. Lighter sunglasses may not be dark enough to protect retinal sensitivity for night vision.
     Therefore, it has long been recognized that military flyers should use sunglasses on sunny days. These
     sunglasses should have a visible luminance transmission of 15 percent or less. Sunglasses identified on the
     authorized protective eyewear list should provide adequate protection for night vision if they are worn
     consistently when outdoors in bright sunlight.

148        TC 3-04.1-4  18 March 2026


---

                                                                                                                   Rotary-Wing Night Flight

Bright Lights

     4-10. Exposure to bright sunlight also has a cumulative and adverse effect on dark adaptation. Reflective
     surfaces such as sand, snow, water, and manmade structures intensify this condition. For example, exposure
     to intense sunlight for 2 to 5 hours decreases visual sensitivity for up to 5 hours and also decreases the rate
     of dark adaptation and degree of night visual acuity.

Flash Blindness

             Note. Dark adaptation recovery time depends on duration and intensity of the exposure.

     4-11. While dark adaptation of the rods develops rather slowly over a period of 30 to 45 minutes, it can be
     lost in a few seconds of exposure to bright light. If the eyes are exposed to bright light after dark adaptation,
     their sensitivity is temporarily impaired. The degree of impairment depends on the intensity and duration of
     the exposure. Brief flashes from high-intensity, white xenon strobe lights commonly used as aircraft anti-
     collision lights have little effect on night vision because the energy pulses are of such short duration, lasting
     only milliseconds. Exposure of 1 second or longer to a flare or searchlight, however, can seriously impair
     night vision. Depending on brightness (intensity) and exposure duration or after repeated exposures, complete
     dark adaptation recovery time can range from 5 to 45 minutes or longer. Accordingly, during night operations
     aircrew members should avoid bright lights or protect one eye. Dark adaptation is an independent process in
     each eye. Even though a bright light may shine into one eye, the other eye will retain its dark adaptation if it
     is protected from the light. Aircrew members should avoid looking at flares, flames, or gun flashes to avoid
     temporary flash blindness. If a supplemental light must be used, it should be as dim as possible while still
     being readily usable (the lowest easily readable level) and should only be used for the shortest possible period.

TYPES OF VISION

     4-12. Types of vision are related to the light level—photopic, mesopic, scotopic (figure 4-2). They relate to
     the level of detail available to the aviator under different conditions. These concepts are more fully explained
     from a medical perspective in TC 3-04.93.

                                                      Figure 4–2. Light levels

PHOTOPIC VISION

     4-13. Photopic vision is experienced during daylight or under high levels of artificial illumination (figure 4-
     3, page 150). Cones concentrated in the fovea centralis are primarily responsible for vision in bright light.
     Due to the high-level light condition, rod cells are bleached out and become less effective. Sharp image
     interpretation and color vision are characteristics of photopic vision.

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  149


---

Chapter 4

                                                   Figure 4–3. Photopic vision

MESOPIC VISION

     4-14. There is a common misconception that the rods are used only at night and the cones only during the
     day. Actually, both rods and cones function simultaneously over a wide range of light intensity levels. The
     transition zone between photopic and scotopic vision, where the level of illumination is equivalent to twilight
     or dusk, is called mesopic vision (figure 4-4). It is experienced at dawn, dusk, and under full moonlight. The
     brightness output from NVG also falls within this range. Visual acuity steadily decreases with declining light.
     Color vision is reduced or degraded as light levels decrease and the cones become less effective. The central
     or night-blind spot becomes more apparent as cone cell sensitivity is lost. Mesopic vision can be the most
     dangerous visual conditions for crewmembers. How degraded the ambient light condition is determines what
     type of scanning or viewing technique crewmembers should use to detect objects and maintain safe and
     incident-free flight.

                                                   Figure 4–4. Mesopic vision

SCOTOPIC VISION

     4-15. Scotopic vision is experienced in low light environments such as partial moonlight and starlight
     conditions (figure 4-5, page 151). Cones become ineffective in these conditions (approximately 50 percent
     illumination and below), causing poor resolution in detail. Visual acuity decreases to 20/200 or less, and
     color perception is lost. Scotopic vision degrades color perception to shades of black, gray, and white unless
     the light source is of adequate intensity to stimulate the cones. The central or night-blind spot is fully evident.
     Scanning, off-center and peripheral vision are used while viewing with scotopic vision.

150        TC 3-04.1-4  18 March 2026


---

                                                                                                                   Rotary-Wing Night Flight

                                                   Figure 4–5. Scotopic vision

RETINAL BLIND SPOTS

     4-16. There are two areas in the retina that can lead to impaired night vision. These two blind spots are
     outlined below and can have a significant impact on flight operations. They are more fully described in TC
     3-04.93.
     4-17. The day blind spot is offset from the center of the retina (figure 4-6). It is where the optic nerve attaches
     to the retina. No cones or rods are present at the attachment point. It is slightly smaller than the night-blind
     spot. Viewing with binocular vision compensates for the day blind spot, as each eye overlaps the other when
     viewing. Note that this compensation no longer exists for aviators using a single occluding monocular, such
     as the helmet display unit (HDU) used in the AH-64.

                                              Figure 4–6. Day blind spot

4-18. The night-blind spot occurs due to the total absence of rod cells in the fovea (figure 4-7, page 152). It
occurs when the cone cells become inactive in low light conditions and involves an area from 5 to 10 degrees
wide in the center of the visual field. It is necessary to look about ten degrees to one side or the other of the
object in question, allowing the rods to detect the object. At these low light levels, though, the object tends
to fade away when stared at for longer than a few seconds. This is because the rhodopsin reaches chemical
equilibrium and stops transmitting visual information. The night-blind spot causes difficulty when
individuals do not move their head or eyes but continue to look directly at or near an object. The size of the
objects that can be hidden by the night-blind spot increases as the distance between the observer and object
increases. The night-blind spot is compensated for by using proper scanning techniques and off-center
viewing.

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  151

Chapter 4

                                                   Figure 4–7. Night-blind spot

SECTION II – NIGHT VISION SENSORS

     4-19. Sensors that aid aircrews in low light operations continuously improve as new technology is developed.
     However, aircrews should always develop a secondary scan, especially in critical situations, to decrease the
     risk of adverse sensor failures.

SENSOR TYPES

     4-20. The two types of aviation night vision devices used by Army Aviation are image intensifier systems
     and thermal imaging systems.
     4-21. Image intensifier systems amplify both visible and near infrared (IR) light energy (figure 4-8). They
     greatly improve night vision but require some degree of light to function. Their performance is degraded
     during low ambient light and adverse weather conditions.

                                              Figure 4–8. What sensors can see

ELECTROMAGNETIC SPECTRUM

     4-22. Just as a radio must be tuned to receive specific frequencies, NVG, thermal sensors and human eyes
     are each sensitive to a specific wavelength or frequency range of the electromagnetic (EM) spectrum. The
     optical band covered by visible light is a relatively small portion of the entire EM spectrum. NVG and thermal
     sensors such as FLIR operate at different but complementing regions of the EM spectrum. Energy in the
     visual and short-wave IR portion of the EM spectrum are normally referred to as light, while energy in the
     mid and far IR bands are normally referred to as thermal or heat energy. This is because the light energy is
     primarily reflected from the observed object while the thermal energy is primarily emitted by the object.

152        TC 3-04.1-4  18 March 2026


---

                                                                                                                   Rotary-Wing Night Flight

IMAGE INTENSIFIERS

     4-23. An image intensifier is an electronic device that amplifies light energy (figure 4-9). The Army only
     uses one image intensifier system for flight operations—the aviator night vision imaging system (ANVIS).

                                                  Figure 4–9. Image intensifier

AVIATOR NIGHT VISION IMAGING SYSTEM

     4-24. The ANVIS is a helmet-mounted or hand-held passive binocular that provides the capability for pilots
     to fly in terrain flight modes at night. The ANVIS is used with the HGU-56/P helmet and the AH-64 Apache
     integrated helmet and display sighting system (IHADSS) when equipped with an ANVIS helmet mount. This
     system amplifies ambient light so the viewed scene becomes clearly visible to the operator.

SYSTEM PERFORMANCE

     4-25. Visual acuity for aviators can be defined as the ability to resolve details in the visual scene. Visual
     acuity is measured according to what the unaided viewer can see at specific distances. Normal daytime visual
     acuity with the unaided human eye is 20/20. This means that the viewer can distinguish at a distance of 20
     feet what a normal observer can distinguish at 20 feet. A visual acuity of 20/40 means that the viewer can
     distinguish at 20 feet what a normal observer can distinguish at 40 feet, indicating that individual’s eyesight
     is not as clear as standard daylight vision.

     4-26. The visual acuity of ANVIS is directly related to the light level available to the image intensifier. As
     available light decreases, ANVIS visual acuity declines with it. Visual acuity maximizes at 100 percent
     illumination (full moon conditions), degrading slowly until available illumination reaches approximately 50
     percent, or ½ moon. As illumination drops below 50 percent, visual acuity degrades more rapidly, causing
     the halo effect around light sources to be more pronounced. As illumination levels drop below 30 percent
     scintillation (sparkling) becomes apparent. Visual acuity is at its lowest at 0 percent illumination (starlight
     conditions), with a fully overcast sky, and no cultural (manmade) sources of illumination.

     4-27. Generally speaking, visual acuity at 100 percent illumination and a high-contrast environment is
     approximately 20/25 as described above. This means that the aviator's visual acuity is slightly lower than
     'normal' daytime vision. Under these conditions, aviators should be able to perceive small obstacles, such as
     wires. It should be stressed that acuity for ANVIS operators is below daytime acuity, even under optimum
     conditions.

     4-28. Under the lowest light conditions (0 percent illumination, with overcast skies and no cultural lighting)
     ANVIS visual acuity is approximately 20/70. Under these conditions, aviators may not be able to perceive
     large objects, such as standard power poles.

     4-29. Low-contrast environments (such as snow-covered territory, sandy deserts, large bodies of water, or
     grassy hills) degrade visibility, making it difficult to distinguish features of the terrain. In these environments,
     ANVIS visual acuity can deteriorate to 20/200 or worse.

SYSTEM FUNCTION

     4-30. The image intensifier is the heart of the ANVIS. It is designed around the principle that it is impossible
     to amplify light. Light entering the intensifier is converted to electricity. The electrical energy is then
     amplified and reconverted into light. The image intensifier is composed of four components: photocathode,

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  153


---

Chapter 4

     micro-channel plate, phosphor screen, and fiber-optic inverter. System function is fully explained in TM 11-
     5855-313-10 but generally works as follows (figure 4-10):

            Figure 4–10. Aviator’s night vision imaging system operational sequence
     • Light energy, consisting of photons, enters the objective lens and is inverted and focused onto a

          photocathode that is responsive to both visible and near IR radiation.
     • Photons striking the photocathode are converted to a proportionate number of electrons. Electrons

          are accelerated away from the photocathode to the microchannel plate via an electrical field
          produced by the power supply.
     • The microchannel plate is a thin wafer of tiny glass tubes that are tilted at a slight angle (figure 4-
          11). Electrons enter these tubes and strike the walls. This reentry reaction exponentially increases
          the number of electrons created.

                                          Figure 4–11. Microchannel plate
     • These increased numbers of electrons are then accelerated to the phosphor screen (figure 4-12). The

          phosphor screen creates a lighted image proportional to the number and velocity of the electrons
          striking it.

     Figure 4–12. Phosphor screen

                                                                                                                   Rotary-Wing Night Flight

          • The image is then passed through a fiber-optic inverter to rotate the image 180 degrees to correct
                the image for the viewer. The image is focused onto the viewer's eye through an eyepiece lens.

POWER SUPPLY

     4-31. The power supply provides automatic brightness control that automatically adjusts microchannel plate
     voltage to maintain image brightness within set limits for the viewer. Another feature is bright source
     protection which reduces the voltage to the photocathode when exposed to bright light sources. This feature
     protects the image intensifier from damage and enhances its life. Both features reduce ANVIS resolution.

MINUS BLUE FILTER

     4-32. The objective lens contains a "minus-blue" coating. This is a special coating on the objective lenses
     that reduces interference from the instrument panel and NVG-compatible supplemental cockpit lights. It
     makes the ANVIS "blind" to the lighting so the glare does not interfere with viewing outside the aircraft. The
     minus blue filter is the primary difference between the ANVIS-6, military ANVIS-9 (F-4949), and civilian
     ANVIS-9.

HALO

     4-33. The halo is a hazy ring surrounding light sources in the NVG (figure 4-13). The halo in the ANVIS is
     primarily the result of electron scatter between the photocathode and the micro-channel plate. A significant
     amount of moisture in the air may slightly intensify this effect.

                                                      Figure 4–13. Halo effect

SYSTEM COUNTERWEIGHTS

     4-34. ANVIS is frequently used with a counterweight system (figure 4-14). This system is designed to offset
     the downward pull of the ANVIS and keep the helmet correctly positioned on the wearer's head. The
     counterweight may not exceed 22 ounces and must be in the weight bag to allow proper separation in the
     event of a hard landing. See TM 11-5855-313-10 for full information.

               Figure 4–14. Counterweights

HEADS-UP DISPLAY SYSTEMS

     4-35. There are several aircraft systems designed to provide the pilot and copilot with HUDs superimposed
     on the real world ANVIS image. They are intended to provide the pilot and copilot a means of monitoring
     essential operation of the helicopter without checking the cockpit displays, allowing them to remain focused
     on flight conditions outside the aircraft.

     4-36. HUDs provide significantly improved situational awareness but must be used properly. It is important
     for the operator to adjust system brightness to match the flight environment. When flying in a dark or low
     contrast environment, it may become necessary to reduce system brightness or turn it off temporarily in order
     to see clearly. Similarly, if the system brightness is too low, it may be difficult or impossible to read the
     display in a high-light environment.

WEATHER

     4-37. The presence of thin clouds that progress into thicker ones can hide terrain features and creates a severe
     hazard for NVG operations. Low clouds lying upon and between hills present a particularly dangerous
     situation due to the inability of the aircrew to distinguish between the clouds and the terrain. The aircrew
     must be alert for a gradual reduction in light level and notice the obstruction of the moon and the stars. The
     less visible the moon and stars are, the heavier the cloud coverage. If the NVG image becomes grainy and
     begins to scintillate (sparkle), this is an indication that weather may be causing a low ambient light condition.
     Since NVG can 'see' through a limited amount of obscurant, IIMCs are a real possibility under these
     conditions. Aircrew members must be prepared to respond accordingly.

VISIBILITY RESTRICTIONS

     4-38. Visibility restrictions (caused by fog, rain, dust, haze, or smoke) reduce the effectiveness of the ANVIS.
     The low altitudes used during terrain flight are especially susceptible to the effects of such visibility
     restrictions. As the temperature-dew point spread narrows, fog is more likely to occur. NVDs permit an
     aviator to see through some obscurations to an extent. Once an aviator realizes the severity of the obscuration,
     it may be too late to do anything other than execute IIMC recovery. The following conditions indicate
     restricted visibility:

          • Loss of celestial lights. For example, overcast cloud cover may cause the moon and stars to fade or
                disappear.

          • Loss of ground lights. City or rural lights fade due to obscuration.
          • Reduced ambient light levels. Obscuration reduces forecast light levels. The exact amount of

                reduction varies with conditions.
          • Reduced visual acuity. Best-case visual acuity is based on high ambient illumination, high contrast,

                and clear visibility. Visual acuity may be reduced depending on the type and amount of ambient
                light and obscuration.
          • Increased halo effect. As the background illumination decreases, halos in the ANVIS field of view
                become more pronounced, indicating reduced system acuity.
          • Scintillation. As the background illumination decreases, system video noise becomes visible. Image
                scintillation is this noise signal seen by the crewmember as a sparkling effect.

WEAPONS EFFECTS

     4-39. Forward firing ordnance have immediate adverse effects on the ANVIS image due to the activation of
     bright source protection within the ANVIS power supply. The effects of ordnance fired from other aircraft
     or ground forces vary greatly, depending on the type/size, proximity, and aspect to the aircraft. Secondary
     explosions and fires within the target area can gain down the ANVIS, causing a loss of detail within the target
     area. Smoke amplifies this effect by limiting visibility and diffusing the light and heat. The distraction
     provided the flickering ANVIS display can be very disorienting. Aviators must remember that their mission
     takes precedence, and their primary concern is aircraft control. It may become necessary to adjust field of
     view or transfer control to the side of the aircraft away from the interference.

THERMAL SYSTEMS

     4-40. Thermal imaging systems "see" objects in the field of view by detecting small differences in the object's
     temperature in relation to the background. As a result, their performance is not related to the ambient
     illumination, as for an image intensifier. Performance is degraded by atmospheric conditions to a far smaller
     degree.

PRINCIPLE OF OPERATION

     4-41. A thermal sensor converts the thermal energy from the outside scene into electrical signals (figure 4-
     15). These signals are then processed and converted into an image that can be seen by the aircrew. Thermal
     energy first passes through a window that filters out all but the desired wavelength of energy. An IR telescope
     then focuses the energy onto a scanning assembly. The scanner searches the thermal scene and transmits it
     to a checkerboard of cooled sensors. A computer compiles the information from this sensor array into a video
     image.

                                                  Figure 4–15. Thermal sensor

     4-42. Currently, Army attack and reconnaissance helicopters utilize the FLIR for target acquisitions during
     day and night operations. The AH-64D/E modernized pilot night vision system (MPNVS) and modernized
     target acquisition device system (MTADS) are passive systems which sense and display various levels of IR
     energy radiating from objects. This allows operators to view objects regardless of visible light levels required
     for unaided and aided operations. The effectiveness of the FLIR depends on the difference in detected IR
     radiation between an object and its background. Effectiveness also depends on atmospheric considerations,
     specifically, the degree of obscuration present between the system and the object. FLIR is most effective
     when a large difference in IR radiation exists between an object and its background and when obscuration is
     minimal. In the AH-64, MTADS is the primary flight sensor for the co-pilot gunner (CPG) (front seat) and
     is also used for targeting. The MTADS is used as a backup to the MPNVS if the pilot's (back seat) MPNVS
     fails and the pilot still wants to fly, that aviator takes the MTADS from the CPG. However, this is not always
     the case; often the pilot passes control of the aircraft to the CPG, while that person figures out what went
     wrong with the MPNVS. At which time the CPG would use the MTADS to fly the aircraft. Aviators should
     consult the appropriate aircraft operator's manual for specific operating instructions.

MINIMUM RESOLVABLE TEMPERATURE

     4-43. A thermal system's ability to detect temperature differences is referred to as the minimum resolvable
     temperature. This is the lowest equivalent thermal difference between an object and its background that can
     be resolved, or seen, by an observer through a thermal system. Thermal sensors "see" objects in the field of
     view by detecting small differences in the object's temperature in relation to the background. If the thermal
     sensor is not sensitive enough, objects are not easily detected. Visual discrimination of objects in the thermal
     scene is made possible when objects have a different radiated temperature (energy) than their immediate
     backgrounds. If there were no difference between the radiated temperature of an object and its background,

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  157


---

Chapter 4

     the object would have no contrast and would not be distinguishable from its background. It would, in effect,
     be invisible.

FORWARD LOOKING INFRARED OPTIMIZATION

     4-44. Detailed procedures for optimizing are found in appropriate operator’s manuals. Generally, FLIR
     optimization is a combination of level and gain settings, which produces the most detail in the displayed
     image. It is equivalent to the brightness control on a cathode ray tube. From these settings, an adjustment of
     either control in either direction produces less detail or degrades the image quality of the FLIR. The level
     and gain controls on the display control panel are used to adjust the FLIR sensor. Proper adjustment of FLIR
     provides the highest possible resolution picture for the operating environment at time of adjustment. If the
     FLIR is operating properly, scene content—such as terrain and metal buildings, temperature, humidity,
     atmospheric conditions, and range to the viewed objects—will determine the image quality.

     4-45. Considerations for FLIR optimization are—
          • The FLIR should be allowed to cool to proper operating temperatures before optimizing.
          • The aviator selects a scene that is potentially rich in detail or best represents the planned flight
                environment.
          • The aviator selects the desired polarity.
          • Only one control should be adjusted at a time: never simultaneously.

     4-46. To accomplish FLIR optimization, the aviator fully decreases level and gain controls, which completely
     darkens the display. Level control is increased until the display just begins to brighten, then gain control is
     advanced until obvious variations in shading appear in the display and stop the advance. The aviator then
     makes minute adjustments in level and gain controls to complete the optimization process.

     4-47. FLIR optimization described above is appropriate only for the scene viewed and existing atmospheric
     conditions at the time of the optimization. Generally, changes in atmospheric environment and scene content
     require only minor adjustments of level and gain controls after FLIR is initially optimized. To ensure
     effectiveness of FLIR, aviators should continually optimize the FLIR image. Aviators must clearly
     understand and effectively practice the principles of FLIR optimization.

ATMOSPHERIC EFFECTS

     4-48. Atmosphere is the most important environmental factor effecting the performance of thermal sensors
     (figure 4-16). The atmosphere absorbs or scatters thermal energy, reducing the level of energy reaching the
     sensor. The impact of these mechanisms on the thermal image varies based upon its operating range.

                                              Figure 4–16. Atmospheric effects

     4-49. For example, FLIR visibility through diesel fog or oil smoke is very good. However, phosphorous
     smoke from a White Phosphorous (WP) marking round or flares significantly hinders thermal transmission.
     Therefore, WP markers are easily seen by a FLIR. There are also special obscurants designed to block thermal
     signatures and serve as thermal camouflage.

---

                                                                                                                   Rotary-Wing Night Flight

ATMOSPHERIC ABSORPTION

     4-50. Atmospheric absorption is the primary source of atmospheric interference. Water in the atmosphere
     (humidity) absorbs IR energy, preventing it from reaching the sensor. In general, the greater the absolute
     humidity, the greater the IR absorption (especially in the far IR band). Therefore, the quality of the thermal
     image depends heavily on humidity. A dry mid-latitude winter day is almost completely transparent to far IR
     energy, whereas a wet tropical atmosphere becomes an effective wall that severely hinders the operational
     capability of the sensor.

SCATTERING

     4-51. Scattering is second to absorption in its impact on thermal performance. As light and thermal energy
     travels through the atmosphere it can strike a particle, thereby changing the path of the energy. Large particles
     such as dust or smog scatter energy by reflection. The wavelengths detected by thermal sensors are about 10
     times longer than those detected by NVG. Therefore, thermal systems can be very effective in conditions that
     greatly hinder the human eye and NVG, such as smoke or haze.

     4-52. Because thermal sensors enable the crew to see through obscurants such as fog, rain, haze, and smoke,
     they may fail to initially detect obscurations. Aircrew members must remain alert for any decrease in image
     quality that might indicate increasing density in the obscuration and avoid IIMCs.

SAND AND DUST

     4-53. Unlike precipitation that creates a uniform temperature over a period of time, the effects of sand or dust
     will diminish as their atmospheric concentration diminishes. The FLIR may continue to see "hotter" objects
     through sand or dust clouds. While there may be limited information provided for navigation, targeting
     capability may still be retained. If the particle size is small, FLIR performance may not even be impacted.

     4-54. During takeoff or landing operations, however, dust presents a significant problem for thermal sensors.
     Aviators must exercise caution when encountering an environment in which significant levels of dust may
     occur.

LIGHTS

     4-55. Lights visible to the unaided eye at night are normally not visible through the FLIR. Crewmembers can
     compensate for this by looking for lights with the unaided eye.

INFRARED CROSSOVER

     4-56. The time of day when soil, water, and concrete thermal radiation are nearly equal is known as IR
     crossover (figure 4-17, page 160). During the day/night cycle, objects in the environment heat and cool at
     different rates. Large dense objects such as medium sized rocks and non-operating armored targets heat and
     cool slowly. Less dense objects such as blades of grass, tree leaves, bushes and the surface layer of the ground
     itself are examples of objects that heat and cool quickly. Crossover for soil, water, and concrete usually
     occurs twice in 24 hours. Soil and concrete do not crossover with vegetation; however, vegetation and water
     do crossover. The timing of the IR crossovers is greatly influenced by environmental factors and can be
     completely unpredictable. An example of this would be a desert environment, where crossover may occur
     several times in one day and then not again for several days in a row. Several successive days of cold, damp
     weather can tend to cool all of the objects in the environment to the point that the difference between the
     temperatures of the objects and the background is very small. Details in the scene are much more difficult to
     detect, and objects are much more difficult to see. Modern thermal sensors have very low minimum
     resolvable temperature, enabling them to detect very small temperature differences in a thermal scene. This
     significantly reduces the impact of IR crossover.

DEPTH PERCEPTION AND DISTANCE ESTIMATION

     4-57. The FLIR system greatly affects depth perception and distance estimation. To help overcome the loss
     of peripheral vision cues and the two-dimensional image, flight information is symbolically superimposed
     on the FLIR image. An aviator must rely on flight symbology and monocular cues for accurate depth
     perception and distance estimation.

COLOR DISCRIMINATION

     4-58. Color discrimination of objects is absent due to the operational properties of FLIR. Color is based on
     energy which falls into the visible light spectrum. FLIR images are produced by detecting IR energy radiating
     from objects and do not require visible light. FLIR displays are monochromatic and shading is used to display
     different levels of detected energy. The unaided eye is able to distinguish the color of lights that are bright
     enough.

PARALLAX EFFECT

     4-59. This occurs in a MPNVS due to the relative distance between the FLIR sensor and the HDU. The FLIR
     sensor is contained within the MPNVS turret located on the nose of the aircraft, while the HDU is positioned
     in front of the aviator's eye. The MPNVS turret is located approximately 10 feet forward and 3 feet below
     the aviator's design-eye position. In both crewmember positions, the thermal scene viewed on the HDU is
     obtained from the physical perspective point of the FLIR sensor. The aviator flying with the MPNVS views
     with the FLIR sensor, not with their unaided eye. Attempts to correlate the thermal scene viewed through the
     HDU with the actual scene viewed using the unaided eye can result in an apparent difference in the location
     of objects within the scene.

     4-60. In figure 4-18, page 161, the aviator has turned their head 90 degrees to the right, and the MPNVS
     turret is pointed 90 degrees to the right. An object (tree) is located at A in the illustration. The FLIR sensor
     views the tree in the center of the FOV along the line-of-sight; however, the aviator's unaided eye would not
     see the tree in the center of their FOV, rather slightly left of the aviator’s FOV. The parallax effect increases
     with the turret offset angle and the relative closeness of obstacles to the aircraft. The aviator must relate their
     view of the MPNVS scene between the origin of the image (MPNVS turret) and the aviators’ seating position.

BINOCULAR RIVALRY

     4-61. Binocular rivalry describes the competition between the MPNVS aided eye and an unaided eye, while
     an aviator is flying with monocular-equipped MPNVS. This rivalry can be described as an undirected
     attention shift of an aviator's desired visual reference point (HDU display) to an undesired point or scene, or
     vice versa. The frequency and length of these occurrences depend on several variables including HDU
     luminance, ambient scene luminance, HDU scene complexity, ambient scene complexity, and to some
     degree, eye dominance at early stages in training. Aviators are accustomed to using both eyes while
     performing flight duties. The MPNVS monocular display is positioned in front of only one eye (aided eye),
     leaving the other eye unaided. Difficulty arises when an aviator is forced to manage the direction of both
     eyes, while maintaining a high degree of concentration with the MPNVS. This is coupled with the need to
     absorb any information observed by the unaided eye such as caution lights or a flare outside the cockpit. The
     goal is to prevent an uncommanded shift by either eye. To control or prevent binocular rivalry, an aviator
     should select, through experimentation, one of three cockpit lighting configurations—floodlights bright, dim,
     or off. During night flights, external light interferences are commonplace, so the aircrew should plan its
     flights to eliminate disturbances from known light sources. A high degree of concentration is required when
     managing visual perception with MPNVS. Even experienced aviators are susceptible to binocular rivalry.
     Adequate crew rest aids in overcoming this problem. Using a tinted visor periodically also assists in reducing
     visual distractions. If all else fails, an aviator may have to close one eye until the rivalry subsides.

SCANNING TECHNIQUES

     4-62. Proper scanning techniques are essential during FLIR night flights. To overcome limited FOV (30
     degrees by 40 degrees) and loss of peripheral cues, an aviator must use a continual scanning pattern during
     terrain flight. With a moving aircraft, the scan is performed by looking left and right of the aircraft centerline
     while maintaining reference with the symbolic head tracker. An aviator bases the length of time and
     frequency of the scanning pattern on terrain type, obstacles, airspeed, and scene content quality of the
     MPNVS. Aviators use close cues to determine obstacle clearance altitude, airspeed, and closure rates, as well
     as midrange and far cues to evaluate route trends and patterns such as direction, turns, and obstacles. Avoid
     overflying close-in cues, maintain obstacle clearance, and use aided and unaided eyes to detect and avoid
     obstacles.

     4-63. An aviator can overcome the inability of FLIR to see lights by incorporating the unaided eye into the
     scanning pattern. While scanning, periodically changing FLIR sensor polarity assists in distinguishing
     obstacles such as aircraft, tree branches, and power poles. These may be difficult to detect because direct
     current restoration (horizon blooming) washes out the upper portion of the video image during rolling
     maneuvers when the bank angle is increased.

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  161

Chapter 4

     4-64. Finally, an aviator needs practice and experience to obtain maximum visual information from both the
     aided and unaided eyes. An aviator must learn to correctly interpret and use flight symbology for aircraft
     control. Reliance on imagery alone or dependence on unaided vision is not enough and results in erratic
     aircraft control. Unaided peripheral vision in the aided eye may be distracting until an aviator learns to use
     primarily FLIR cues and symbology, and disregard unwanted peripheral distractions.

SPATIAL DISORIENTATION

     4-65. Aviators avoid maneuvers requiring large bank angles or rapid attitude changes. These maneuvers tend
     to induce spatial disorientation. An aviator flying with MPNVS may become disoriented and experience an
     unusual attitude when the pilot has visual reference with the surface of the earth with the FLIR sensor. This
     also occurs when reference is lost due to FLIR image degradation or sensor failure. Proper scanning
     techniques—using a slow, purposeful head movement and positive aircraft control with the proper
     symbology mode—aids in preventing spatial disorientation. Adequate crew coordination should be
     preplanned and prebriefed to assist aviators in recovering from spatial disorientation. Regardless of the
     symbology mode being employed at the time of disorientation—hover, bob-up, transition, or cruise—the
     initial recovery steps are the same. The crew orients the MPNVS turret toward the aircraft nose and minimizes
     head movement during the recovery. The head tracker should be located and cross-checked with the line-of-
     sight reticle. The crew can use the remaining flight symbology to complete reorientation and recovery.

AIRSPEED AND GROUND-SPEED LIMITATIONS

     4-66. Aviators using FLIR tend to overfly their capability to see. To avoid obstacles, aviators must understand
     the relationship among the system's visual range, atmospheric conditions, and airspeed. With the limited
     visual range of FLIR, aviators must exercise extreme care when using the systems during terrain flight modes.
     With poor atmospheric conditions and subsequent poor thermal resolution, a reduction in ground speed may
     be appropriate. Object acquisition and identification are related to atmospheric conditions and thermal
     contrast. The variables affecting the ability to see with FLIR include—

          • IR crossover.
          • FLIR sensor optimization.
          • Minimum resolvable temperature.
          • Aviator's proficiency and capabilities.

WEATHER

     4-67. FLIR systems have the ability to see through most obscurations; however, aviators flying with MPNVS
     should be aware they may fail to detect IMCs. If the aircraft has entered IMCs, an aviator must be careful not
     to overfly FLIR capabilities and to continue slowing as conditions degrade. Increasing graininess and
     reduction in scene quality indicate deteriorating weather such as a denser obscuration or equalizing
     temperature in the viewed scene. When an aviator recognizes this restricted visibility, reoptimizing the FLIR
     is attempted using level and gain controls. If this does not work, an aviator must turn away from the weather
     conditions, land, or execute IIMC recovery procedures.

TARGET DETECTION

     4-68. Detection of targets at night using the FLIR system is fairly easy; however, identification of those
     targets is often difficult. To help alleviate this situation, the pilot can assist the copilot gunner in detection by
     using MPNVS. The primary duty, however, is to fly the aircraft. Because the MPNVS has no magnification
     capability, the maximum range an aviator can detect is highly dependent on size of the object, thermal
     temperatures and atmospheric conditions. The MTADS FLIR is the primary night acquisition source for the
     AH-64D/E. It is a passive night viewing device with four different FOVs. The copilot gunner's ability to
     optimize and operate the MTADS FLIR directly influences the capability to detect targets. The black/white
     hot feature allows pilots to change the way the temperature differences are displayed. This feature can
     enhance target detection and target recognition. The white-hot setting displays a thermal image of the scene
     in which hot objects are displayed with positive contrast, so appear bright. In white hot, hot targets such as
     tanks are generally more apparent than in black hot because the bright end of the gray scale is usually more
     noticeable than the dark end. Since targets are typically warmer than their background, white-hot produces
     bright targets that can generally be detected at greater ranges. Black hot tends to produce a more natural scene
     for pilotage and terrain recognition purposes (figure 4-19, page 163).

WEAPONS

     4-69. During rocket firing, the motor burn from the rocket illuminates the cockpit area letting the aviator see
     some sparkling effect to the front of the aircraft. Other than this momentary distraction to the unaided eye,
     the crew should not experience any adverse effects. When the aircrew member fires the 30-millimeter cannon,
     the muzzle blast may distract the unaided eye if the gun is fired off axis. Crew coordination and
     communication can minimize this temporary distraction. While firing Hellfire missiles, the crew experiences
     a temporary illumination of the cockpit area similar to rocket firings. This temporary distraction from the
     flight motor of the missile does not affect either crewmember's aided eye, which is already adapted to
     photopic vision.

SOURCES OF THERMAL ENERGY

     4-70. There are different sources of thermal heat that require consideration by mission planners. Those listed
     below should be considered during overall mission planning in regard to both protection of organic equipment
     and attack elements.

SOLAR RADIATION

     4-71. Those objects that do not have their own power source obtain most of their thermal energy from the
     sun. Factors that affect available sunlight impact the thermal scene. The two most prominent factors that
     dictate the amount of solar radiation available on a clear day are time of day and time of year. The higher the
     sun is in the sky, the more intense the available solar radiation. Solar elevation coupled with how much of
     the object's surface is exposed to the sun influences the amount of solar radiation absorbed (figure 4-20).

               Figure 4–20. Solar radiation

Chapter 4

FUEL COMBUSTION OR FRICTIONAL HEAT

     4-72. The vast majority of thermal energy is derived from the sun and even synthetic objects appear very
     much like themselves when heated by the sun. However, the thermal signature of a machine can appear to be
     distorted after it has been operating. The heat from areas of artificial heating, such as engine compartments
     or exhausts, appears as hot spots. Frictional heat from moving parts such as wheels or tank tracks usually
     produce a less intense hot spot and can be easily obscured by coverings such as mud or snow. In general,
     these localized hot spots tend to form high contrast areas that aid in detection but could hamper identification
     efforts. Thermal training aids such as the recognition of combat vehicles programs aid in training aircrew to
     identify vehicles and armor according to their thermal signature. Areas involving large amounts of
     combustion, such as burning tires, burning vehicles or burning buildings are visible at great distances and
     can greatly impact the thermal scene.

HEAT TRANSMISSION

     4-73. How an object appears on the FLIR display is based on the amount of exposure the object has had to

   the principle sources of thermal energy (figLureE4F-2T1):SsIoDlarEenergy, fuel combustion, frictional heat and

     thermal reflection, and how easily that object changes temperature as a result. The primary factors involved
     in this transfer of heat energy are reflectance, absorptance, transmittance, and emissivity.

             Figure 4–21. Heat transmission

REFLECTANCE  RIGHT SIDE

     4-74. The tendency of energy to bounce (reflect) off of an object is called reflectance (figure 4-22). Objects

     with a high reflectance (such as a container with a shiny surface) tend to heat more slowly in sunlight.

             Figure 4–22. Reflectance

164          TC 3-04.1-4                     18 March 2026


---

                                                                                                                   Rotary-Wing Night Flight

ABSORPTANCE

     4-75. The tendency of an object to retain energy is called absorptance (figure 4-23). Objects with a high
     absorptance (such as an engine block) hold more of the energy that contacts the object. The ability of an
     object to store heat is also called thermal mass. Thermal mass is determined by the material's temperature,
     mass and type. The greater the amount of heat stored, the hotter the object appears in the thermal sensor. A
     larger object or mass (density times volume) can also store more heat. Some materials store heat very well
     (steel), whereas others store heat very poorly (air). High thermal mass means high heat storage, but it also
     means it takes more heat to change the temperature of an object. While the amount of heat an object holds is
     significant, temperature differences cause differences in the FLIR image, not heat differences. For instance,
     a large rock has a higher heat value than a smaller rock of the same temperature and composition. Except for
     size, the FLIR image of the two rocks would appear identical, even though the larger rock has a higher
     thermal mass. However, the larger rock takes longer to radiate its excess heat than the smaller rock and
     maintains a higher temperature for a longer period of time.

                                                    Figure 4–23. Absorptance

TRANSMITTANCE

     4-76. Objects with a high transmittance value (such as the metal skin of a truck) will transfer heat energy to
     other objects in contact with them, retaining only a portion of that energy internally. (figure 4-24) These
     objects are more likely to display the same temperature to thermal sensor as other objects to which they are
     connected (like the hood of a car).

                                                   Figure 4–24. Transmittance

EMISSIVITY

     4-77. The temperature of an object tends to become the same as its environment. If an object has a higher
     temperature than its surroundings, it becomes cooler. Conversely, if the object is cooler than its surroundings,
     it absorbs energy and become warmer. Whether the object is increasing or decreasing in temperature, it is

18 March 2026  TC 3-04.1-4  165


---

Chapter 4

     always emitting some amount of radiant energy. Different materials transfer energy to balance their
     temperature at different rates. This capacity is known as the emissivity of an object (figure 4-25). Rocks, for
     example, have a higher emissivity than metal objects, so the majority of their thermal signature results from
     self-emission instead of thermal reflectance. Very hot objects emit (radiate) high amounts of thermal energy
     and are easily visible using thermal sensors. The sun is a good example of a thermal radiator. Others include
     the hot metal of a jet engine tailpipe, aerodynamically heated surfaces, motor vehicles, personnel, and terrain.

                                                      Figure 4–25. Emissivity

THERMAL INERTIA

     4-78. Thermal inertia is a combination of thermal mass and thermal resistance and provides a measure of the
     rate at which objects change temperature. Thermal mass determines the amount of heat stored, while thermal
     resistance determines the rate at which the heat flows. An object of high thermal mass and high thermal
     resistance would change temperature slowly and be considered to have high thermal inertia. Examples of this
     include large, dense objects such as big rocks, armored targets, and bodies of water. Lightweight objects such
     as grass, leaves, bushes, and the surface layer of ground heat, cool quickly, and are described as having low
     thermal inertia.

THE THERMAL SCENE

     4-79. The combination of the above factors results in the specific temperature each object in the thermal
     scene presents to the sensor at any given time. The resultant collection of objects (including the earth and the
     sky) is the thermal scene. How visible each object is within that scene is dependent on how significantly that
     object's temperature differs from the background and any other objects nearby.

NVG/THERMAL OPERATIONAL INTEGRATION

     4-80. NVG and thermal sensors work in different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum and with different
     principles of radiated energy, occupying different wavelengths. This can result in one of the NVD systems
     performing better than the other under certain environmental conditions. This complimentary nature works
     well if the user is familiar with the principles of sensor integration. In some instances, both NVDs may be
     adversely affected. Select the sensor appropriate to the mission and flight conditions. The ultimate goal is to
     improve mission safety and effectiveness by using this information during preflight planning and during
     dynamic changes to mission events and environmental conditions once airborne. Aviators should be familiar
     with each sensor's capabilities and limitations and understand each sensor's advantages over the other for
     some tactical applications and during specific environmental conditions.

     4-81. The overall capability of NVG and thermal sensors to use EM energy is a function of both atmospheric
     absorption and scattering. This includes differences in particulate size and concentration. Thermal
     performance can be predicted to some degree by knowing the absolute humidity in the area of interest. NVG
     performance can best be predicted by knowing the illumination level, moon angle and weather. Atmospheric
     conditions can attenuate both NVG and thermal performance. The degree of attenuation depends on factors
     that are difficult to predict and may vary considerably during the mission. In adverse weather, experience
     with the systems and their response to the atmospheric conditions dictates the decision to continue or abort
